boundary_note: Bounded first pass for the frozen Spring Hill record (November 29, 1864) in the Franklin-Nashville Campaign [September-December 1864]. It falls within the Columbia record's interval (TN034, November 24-29) and precedes Franklin (TN036). Campaign-wide marches, returns, reinforcements and multi-action loss totals are context; they are not assigned to one record or added across records. Draft claims do not alter model inputs.

claims.rationale: No inspected return establishes matched personnel at a common opening boundary. The frozen side-specific numerical strength bounds are blank (missing_numeric_strength). No figure in this pass is adopted as a simultaneous opening force.

claims.value: The frozen force text reads the IV and XXIII Corps against the Army of Tennessee with no numbers; the live field reads zeros. Cox says Stanley went to Spring Hill with Wagner's division alone, with six batteries under Bridges, that Bradley's brigade was too isolated to hold alone, and that the Confederates were made to believe they faced a superior force. Hood says he crossed Duck River with Stewart's and Cheatham's corps and Johnson's division in light marching order with one battery to a corps, leaving Lee's other two divisions at Columbia.
claims.rationale: Formations only; no inspected passage gives numbers for the forces at Spring Hill. None is adopted as a matched opening strength; live zeros are not measured absence.

claims.value: Cox says the army's wagon trains had been ordered to Spring Hill and Stanley arrived about noon just in time to prevent their capture, and that Hood's infantry crossed on the pontoon bridge at Davis's Ford after daylight. Hood says his cavalry could not break through the strongly guarded trains and that the Union trains obstructed the road for fifteen miles during the day and much of the night.
claims.rationale: Movement and transport statements from an interested history and report; no transport return inspected.

claims.value: Hood says his object was to turn the Union flank and cut off the force at Columbia by placing troops across the Columbia and Franklin pike at or near Spring Hill, and that Cheatham was ordered to attack at once and take the pike. NPS says the aim was to get astride Schofield's line of communication. Cox says Schofield held on at Columbia to finish obstructing the fords and to ship artillery.
claims.rationale: Stated aims from interested reports and a modern summary.

claims.value: Hood says Cheatham, despite repeated orders, made 'but a feeble and partial attack', and in December wrote that Cheatham had confessed the error and taken all blame. Cox says Hood 'sought to shift the responsibil- ity' onto Cheatham, that a commander present with the head of column could have enforced his orders directly, and that Schofield personally led Ruger's division to Stanley's support. The frozen commanders are General Hood and Major General Schofield.
claims.rationale: The two families assign responsibility for the missed opportunity differently; both attributions are preserved. No listed commander receives automatic sole credit or blame.

claims.value: The frozen and live results read Union victory. NPS says the Federals repulsed a piecemeal attack in late afternoon and the rest of Schofield's command passed through Spring Hill to Franklin in the night. Hood calls it the loss of 'the greatest' opportunity of the campaign. Cox says Wagner's division held Spring Hill until the trains and troops were in motion.
claims.rationale: Retain the original result and engagement interval; later movements and campaign contribution are different measures. No new probabilities or individual causal credit.

open_questions: Stanley's No. 9, Wagner's, Bradley's and Opdycke's reports, Schofield's report, Forrest's No. 252 account of Spring Hill (read in the Murfreesborough selection's source but not cited here), Cheatham's and Cleburne's division reports and Cheatham's 1881 paper cited by Cox remain deferred.

NPS/CWSAC (the live NPS page and the frozen Arnold rows) is one family. Jacob D. Cox's The March to the Sea; Franklin and Nashville (1882) is an interested history by the commander of the Twenty-third Corps' Third Division (and, at Franklin, of both divisions of that corps) that draws on official papers. Corse's, French's, R. S. Granger's, Doolittle's, Sinclair's, Forrest's, Hood's and Rousseau's reports, printed in Official Records Series I, Volumes XXXIX part 1 and XLV part 1, are separate families of interested accounts; each volume is a shared container, not an additional witness. Report dates are not event times or proof of contemporary knowledge.
No automatic commander attribution, causal campaign score, morale/readiness number or battle/campaign double counting.
